title: Opinion: Amid Immigration Crackdown, Let’s Support School Family Liaisons
summary: On election day, voters sent Democrats into office, up and down the ballot, in typically blue strongholds and in places where it had been hard to imagine Republicans losing power. As citizens cast their votes, many were reckoning with the most visible harms caused by this administration’s immigration policies, including mass raids and unprecedented violence […]
content: On election day, voters sent Democrats into office, up and down the ballot, in typically blue strongholds and in places where it had been hard to imagine Republicans losing power . As citizens cast their votes, many were reckoning with the most visible harms caused by this administration’s immigration policies , including mass raids and unprecedented violence — and the damage this inflicts on children . In the coming months, these candidates — both at the national level and in local communities — will have to confront the consequences of ICE’s unrestrained, violent tactics. For local leaders, that should include recognizing and supporting the people who have been doing the vital work of sustaining immigrant families all along. One place to start is in public schools. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter In the U.S., all students have the legal right to attend school, regardless of their or their parents’ immigration status. As a result, schools have long been vital — although imperfect — spaces for welcoming immigrant families as they lay down roots. Related Post-Election Hope for Immigrant Students Dimmed But Not Dead After Miller Named But it isn’t the law that makes schools welcoming. It is the everyday work of educators. Teachers have shown extraordinary dedication as their students suffer under Trump’s aggressive deportation regime. But there are others — secretaries, family liaisons, and other support staff — who also care for immigrant families, even though their invaluable labor is often hidden from the public eye. In research for my book, Holding On to Home: Immigrant Women and the Promise of Sanctuary , I witnessed how these employees, many of whom were immigrants themselves, were essential to families as they adjusted to a new nation. They connected parents to food pantries, provided guidance about managing exploitative landlords and reiterated legal rights. They arranged transportation, enrolled children in afterschool programs and decoded English learner education. And they listened: to stories of the difficult journeys families made to get to the U.S. safely, to their fears of deportation, to worries about kin in their countries of origin. Yet the poor working conditions for these employees speaks to the societal value we place on women’s labor , especially when that labor entails immigrant women caring for other immigrant women. In the small East Coast city I studied, for instance, family liaisons — school-based positions intended to bridge home and school — were capped at 19 hours, just below the threshold for benefits. The women who filled these jobs worked without district-issued cell phones or computers. They squeezed into closets or begged to borrow offices so they didn’t have to hold sensitive conversations in the middle of the hallway. They never worked just 19 hours a week. A few years later, the city converted the family liaisons positions to full-time roles, a major win. But a liaison with seven years of experience made just $43,000 – 40% less than a teacher with similar experience, and barely enough to live in a city where the average salary hovered around $125,000 and housing costs are among the highest in the nation. City council and school committee members have the power to fund these positions — or not. While the fates of long-term city employees may seem mundane in comparison to the existential threat of unrestrained immigration enforcement, their practices transform schools into places that protect and incorporate immigrant families. Related The Latest Wave of Trump’s Immigration Crackdown Is Again Being Felt in Schools Democrats are heading into power. They will need to address how this presidential administration’s decision to slash funds for the most basic necessities put enormous pressure on local governments to make cuts. One long-time district family liaison I know has already been laid off. For nearly three decades, she conducted home visits for immigrant mothers with new babies, weaving the families into a web of resources. To her close colleagues, she was an essential source of information and best practices. But her work wasn’t deemed valuable to the decisionmakers. The labor of women like this liaison defies easy categorization. It is rarely public, unfolding instead in crowded living rooms, on front porches, in corners of school hallways. All of this makes it harder to recognize how this work safeguards the critical role schools play for immigrant families — and for our society as a whole. In this election, voters chose politicians who vocally oppose Trump’s destructive immigration agenda. Now the new leaders at every level of government need to act. It might not be the most obvious place to start, but providing adequate funding for family liaisons and similar positions in schools and communities is a concrete, actionable way to ensure immigrant families have what they need to thrive. These women’s labor strengthens schools, preserves the fabric of society and makes real the promise of American education.

title: From Bus Routes to Ball Games, Diesel Prices Are Squeezing Montana School Budgets
summary: At Beaverhead County High School in the southwest corner of Montana, superintendent Josh Patterson had a dilemma last month when the school’s football team, the Beavers, qualified for a state playoff game in Whitefish. Patterson had to get students back and forth from Dillon to Whitefish, a roughly 12-hour round-trip bus ride. “ What used to […]
content: This article was originally published in Montana Free Press. At Beaverhead County High School in the southwest corner of Montana, superintendent Josh Patterson had a dilemma last month when the school’s football team, the Beavers, qualified for a state playoff game in Whitefish. Patterson had to get students back and forth from Dillon to Whitefish, a roughly 12-hour round-trip bus ride. “ What used to be a celebration has now become a quick kind of scramble to calculate, ‘Ok, how are we going to afford this?’” Patterson said. And Patterson is not alone in trying to reconcile the high cost of fuel with already strapped school budgets, especially in smaller districts. Rural school districts across the state are coping with the elevated price of diesel , a result of tensions in the international market. Everyday bus routes are partially subsidized by state and county governments, but the majority of the bill is still paid by local school districts. And travel for extracurriculars — think sports or speech and debate teams — receives no direct government subsidies. That means hard choices for rural schools that face long drives to students’ homes and even longer trips for major, statewide competitions. In Dillon, Patterson even considered taking money budgeted for school supplies and books to help pay for the trip to Whitefish. “I’ve got some money allocated for curriculum, for textbooks. And I hate to do this, because that’s a priority, but activities is also a priority to our kids, and it’s one thing that helps keep our kids in school,” Patterson said. He called the prospect of choosing between academics and extracurriculars “unfortunate.” And the hardship isn’t confined to sports. Patterson is also dealing with the rising cost of day-to-day school transportation. In 2025, Patterson estimated that Beaverhead spent between $8,000 and $10,000 on diesel each month. A recent bill for a month’s gas was just over $20,000. “That was rather shocking,” Patterson said. The cost of diesel skyrocketed in March , days after the U.S. launched missiles at Iran. The prolonged conflict has kept the price high. On top of that, fighting between Ukraine and Russia has made the latter less eager to sell diesel on the international market. In Montana, where residents spend 27% more per capita on fuel than other Americans, that’s undercut the bottom line of ranchers, farmers, truckers and everyday motorists. School districts have not been spared. How Montana Funds Public School Transportation A school’s transportation budget breaks down into two categories: regular bus routes and extracurriculars. State and county governments help somewhat with the everyday routes. Extracurriculars, though, are paid for by local districts. Everyday bus routes are partially subsidized by state and county funding, based on a district’s buses and the number of miles each bus travels. And although the Legislature in 2025 increased the amount of money the state kicks in for school transportation, those costs typically far exceed what the government contributes. The remainder falls almost entirely on the local districts . Larry Crowder, executive director of the Montana Rural Education Association, called the bill passed during the last session “a good step forward towards addressing the disparities that were caused by 20 years of no increases.” But even with the Legislature’s bump, the state only covers a portion of everyday transportation costs. Between July 2025 and July 2026, statewide districts budgeted $89 million through local levies for transportation costs. That’s more than twice the $36 million they are expected to receive from state and county subsidies, according to the Montana Superintendent of Public Instruction’s data on school districts’ adopted budgets . In Power, a roughly 200-person community about a half-hour drive northwest of Great Falls, the school district has struggled to fuel three school buses that travel a total of about 280 miles each day. Stephani Johnson, Power School District’s business manager, told MTFP in October that school officials “kind of had an idea” that their fuel bill would be higher than past years when they set their budget this summer. But since July, the price has increased 37% . Johnson said what they planned for may not be enough. “ I don’t think we really planned on it getting this high and potentially going even higher, so we might have to pull some funds from some other accounts to make up for it,” Johnson said. Johnson called it “just kind of a waiting game to see if it does go down, hopefully.” “But it definitely impacts us a lot with the fuel bills,” Johnson said. Chester-Joplin-Inverness Public Schools, situated along the Hi-Line between Havre and Shelby, serves about 220 students in a single building. Superintendent Luke Haggerty told MTFP that he would support even further increases in the reimbursement rates. Haggerty said he was “very grateful” that the 2025 Legislature made changes to reimbursement policy, but he acknowledged the increase wasn’t “enough to really make a huge difference.” “It can be frustrating as a district when you’re seeing the price of everything go up around you, and then your budget’s not going up with it,” Haggerty said. Haggerty said he feels the strain of high diesel prices most acutely when it comes to extracurriculars. The Montana High School Association does offer some support for postseason games, including a $2.50-per-mile reimbursement and a modest per diem for each student. But that doesn’t always add up to much. In March, Chester-Joplin-Inverness sent its boys and girls basketball teams — and a pep band — to a tournament in Missoula. The cost of food, lodging and the three buses going there and back? About $28,000. Haggerty said the Montana High School Association provided a $5,200 reimbursement, about 19% of the total bill. “That was when gas was a lot cheaper too,” Haggerty said. “We’re hopeful we’ll send both teams again this year. Who knows how much it’ll cost.” Related Fewer Than Half of States Require K-12 Native American Education Trying to Make Ends Meet Some rural school systems minimize fuel costs by design, mitigating the recent impact of high diesel prices. For instance, Havre, a north-central town of about 9,000, has maintained two electric school buses for several years. The Sun River Valley School District in Simms, a small community about 23 miles east of Augusta, consolidated its students’ sports transportation by combining middle and high school teams onto a single bus for games and other competitions, superintendent Dave Marzolf told MTFP. Additionally, Marzolf said that the district purchased a 15-passenger van in 2024 that runs on unleaded fuel, and when one bus driver retired, the district reduced its four-bus route to three. While he said that during his 18 years as superintendent he hasn’t seen diesel rise above $6 per gallon, Marzolf said his district was prepared for the higher bills. “ I know we’ll have enough money,” Marzolf said. “A smart superintendent budgets for that kind of stuff at the beginning of the year in August, so we should be pretty close. But yeah, we combine kids and that kind of stuff; it saves a little bit of money.” Patterson, the superintendent at Beaverhead, told MTFP that he wants the Legislature to amend state statutes to allow local districts’ permissive levies, which many already use to fill gaps in regular bus routes, to be an eligible funding source for transportation to extracurricular events. “Our citizens and our constituents support our sports and our activities,” Patterson said. “ Not only are we an activity-driven county here, we’re an activity-driven state,” he added. “If we’re being honest, in Montana, we love our sports and our activities. They keep us going. They are the pulse of our communities, our small towns. The whole town shuts down, and we’re all at the game Friday nights, whether it’s in the gym, on the field, or at the track. So I think it’d be something that our lawmakers could support.” So far, lawmakers haven’t gotten behind the change. The Legislature’s Education Interim Legislative Committee reviewed a bill draft related to school transportation funding in September. That document did not include Patterson’s policy proposal. Montana School Boards Association executive director Lance Melton told MTFP he would prioritize securing more funding for everyday bus routes rather than pushing to allow schools to use local tax base money for extracurriculars. Melton argued that Patterson’s proposal would disproportionately benefit high schools, which transport students for after-school activities a lot more than elementary and middle schools do. “ I think we’ve gotta take care of those regular rates for getting kids to and from school, which affects everybody in the state fairly equally,” Melton said. Melton said that Patterson has a great idea for addressing the issue and agreed that extracurricular activities are an important part of students’ education. But he added that he wants to instead focus on increasing subsidies for daily school transportation. “Fix what’s broken now,” Melton said. “Second step, talk about enhancements.” Paying the Way While Beaverhead didn’t go too far in playoffs — Whitefish won 36-12 — bus fuel for the trip totaled about $600. Patterson said the district paid for it from its activity fund. He is still concerned, though, about how the school is going to pay for more travel the rest of the school year. “ The biggest thing we didn’t account for is just the doubling of the cost of fuel when it comes to activity transportation,” Patterson told MTFP. “ We have a budget for half of what we are seeing now because we was thinking fuel was gonna be around anywhere from $3.25 to $3.50, not $5.50.” Patterson said he hopes to give local communities authority to support extracurriculars, what he describes as the “soul of Montana schools.” “ I think people would understand that need and understand we’re not asking for a lot and that we’re not asking for state money,” Patterson said. “I’m not asking for state money to do this. I’m not asking for money from any other district or region. I’m just asking for the ability to do this locally and do it responsibly.” This story was originally published by Montana Free Press and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

title: Opinion: The Midterm Results Should Be Great for Kids. Full Stop
summary: Normally, post-election prognostication involves sifting through and reading the proverbial tea leaves to divine our new political future. One region may tilt right, but only among older voters, while another state’s new political lean seems to be drifting left due to an influx of young college graduates. But my goodness, the 2026 midterm results are […]
content: Normally, post-election prognostication involves sifting through and reading the proverbial tea leaves to divine our new political future. One region may tilt right, but only among older voters, while another state’s new political lean seems to be drifting left due to an influx of young college graduates. But my goodness, the 2026 midterm results are so heavy, it’s a different sort of project. This time, it’s a little more like sifting through the ashes of a blast crater. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter I mean, South Carolina is sending a Democrat to the Senate? I’m old enough to remember when Sen.-elect Annie Andrews’ seat was held by Strom Thurmond , who famously abandoned the party for the Republicans when the Johnson administration got too woke for his liking (by pushing for major civil rights legislation). What was the (historic) 2026 election for education? Some education analysts have mixed feelings . While many are eager to see some curbs on the Trump administration’s wanton wielding of power, they also worry that the country’s all-but-wholesale repudiation of the Republican Party represents a threat to education reform’s political fortunes. After a shift this seismic, no prognosticator should be too confident about the details of what comes next, but one thing’s clear: The curbing of the Trump administration will be good for children in the United States. That ought to be the guiding light here, right? Those of us who measure our involvement in public education in decades, not years, will remember the days when “putting kids’ interests before adults’ hangups” was the reform movement’s North Star — however imperfectly it embodied that ideal from year to year. That’s how reformers proposed, tested, implemented and adjusted the core elements of their agenda during the first two decades of this century. Tests help measure students’ progress to ensure that they’re on track for mid- and long-term success. Accountability systems linked to those tests — and other educational elements — focus adults’ attention on the public’s academic priorities for our schools. Public choice programs protect families from being trapped if the schools assigned to them based on their ability to purchase housing are particularly dysfunctional. Finally, public choice programs are maximally beneficial for children when participating schools have flexibility to design campuses that work but strict public accountability for demonstrating improved student outcomes. Those things are good for kids. Some of them are more popular with Democrats or with Republicans, but none are exclusively the province of either political party. So it’s understandable that reformers might fret that American voters’ firm rejection of Republicans at every level of government could imperil high-quality charter schools or test-based accountability systems for K–12 schools. And yet, the election results could produce negotiations with Congress that ultimately force the Trump administration to end its lawless, chaotic, violent approach to immigration enforcement. That might not be a classic education reform priority, but it could free tens of thousands of terrified children to go back to school. Related Post-Election Hope for Immigrant Students Dimmed But Not Dead After Miller Named Research indicates that the past 18 months of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, funded through several party-line Republican budget bills, have disrupted learning and spiked absenteeism rates , particularly for Latino students in immigrant communities . And that’s to say nothing of conservatives’ many-fronted attacks on multilingual children’s civil rights, such as White House efforts to reduce the amount of information schools translate for families who do not speak English proficiently, launching a new federal mandate that local Head Start programs teach only in English and more. Republicans didn’t just spend their two years of unified control of the federal government targeting immigrant families and communities — and the U.S. citizens living among them. They passed an enormous school choice tax credit that appears likely to primarily fuel more public funding to private schools with limited oversight at any regulatory level. A recent Brookings analysis predicts that the tax credit will produce widespread waste and implementation problems. Research on private choice programs has been largely discouraging , producing mixed academic results and consistent civil rights concerns . Kids may also benefit from new scrutiny of private choice programs at the state level as well, as Democrats won gubernatorial races in Texas, Iowa, and Ohio — three states with robust private choice programs. title: Opinion: The Midterm Results Should Be Great for Kids. Full Stop

content: Normally, post-election prognostication involves sifting through and reading the proverbial tea leaves to divine our new political future. One region may tilt right, but only among older voters, while another state’s new political lean seems to be drifting left due to an influx of young college graduates. But my goodness, the 2026 midterm results are so heavy, it’s a different sort of project. This time, it’s a little more like sifting through the ashes of a blast crater. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter I mean, South Carolina is sending a Democrat to the Senate? I’m old enough to remember when Sen.-elect Annie Andrews’ seat was held by Strom Thurmond , who famously abandoned the party for the Republicans when the Johnson administration got too woke for his liking (by pushing for major civil rights legislation). What was the (historic) 2026 election for education? Some education analysts have mixed feelings . While many are eager to see some curbs on the Trump administration’s wanton wielding of power, they also worry that the country’s all-but-wholesale repudiation of the Republican Party represents a threat to education reform’s political fortunes. After a shift this seismic, no prognosticator should be too confident about the details of what comes next, but one thing’s clear: The curbing of the Trump administration will be good for children in the United States. That ought to be the guiding light here, right? That’s how reformers proposed, tested, implemented and adjusted the core elements of their agenda during the first two decades of this century. Tests help measure students’ progress to ensure that they’re on track for mid- and long-term success. Accountability systems linked to those tests — and other educational elements — focus adults’ attention on the public’s academic priorities for our schools. Public choice programs protect families from being trapped if the schools assigned to them based on their ability to purchase housing are particularly dysfunctional. Finally, public choice programs are maximally beneficial for children when participating schools have flexibility to design campuses that work but strict public accountability for demonstrating improved student outcomes. Those things are good for kids. Some of them are more popular with Democrats or with Republicans, but none are exclusively the province of either political party. So it’s understandable that reformers might fret that American voters’ firm rejection of Republicans at every level of government could imperil high-quality charter schools or test-based accountability systems for K–12 schools. And yet, the election results could produce negotiations with Congress that ultimately force the Trump administration to end its lawless, chaotic, violent approach to immigration enforcement. That might not be a classic education reform priority, but it could free tens of thousands of terrified children to go back to school. And that’s to say nothing of conservatives’ many-fronted attacks on multilingual children’s civil rights, such as White House efforts to reduce the amount of information schools translate for families who do not speak English proficiently, launching a new federal mandate that local Head Start programs teach only in English and more. Republicans didn’t just spend their two years of unified control of the federal government targeting immigrant families and communities — and the U.S. citizens living among them. They passed an enormous school choice tax credit that appears likely to primarily fuel more public funding to private schools with limited oversight at any regulatory level. A recent Brookings analysis predicts that the tax credit will produce widespread waste and implementation problems. Research on private choice programs has been largely discouraging , producing mixed academic results and consistent civil rights concerns . title: The Wise Rise: How One of Virginia’s Poorest Counties Built Some of Its Best Schools
summary: Wise County, Virginia, is one of the state’s most economically disadvantaged counties. Over the last two decades, its population has shrunk as the coal industry that once supported much of its local economy has declined. And yet, Wise County boasts some of the highest-performing schools in the state. When The 74 went looking for Bright […]
content: Wise County, Virginia, is one of the state’s most economically disadvantaged counties. Over the last two decades, its population has shrunk as the coal industry that once supported much of its local economy has declined. And yet, Wise County boasts some of the highest-performing schools in the state. When The 74 went looking for Bright Spots schools that get strong reading scores despite high poverty rates, four out of five Wise elementary schools made our list, including St. Paul Elementary, our highest-ranked school across all of Virginia. Today, Wise posts excellent scores across grades and subjects , but it wasn’t always outstanding. The graph below shows how its students compared to the rest of Virginia on third-grade reading. When Virginia first administered state tests in the late 1990s, Wise students performed a bit worse than their peers across the state. But over time, they went from underperforming, to slightly overperforming, to significantly overperforming. I like to call this “The Wise Rise.” Oh, and Wise is getting these results on a shoestring budget. In the 2024-25 school year, Wise spent just $12,658 per student, $4,100 less than the state average. So what explains The Wise Rise? Learning From What Works The Wise story starts in the early 2000s, when the federal No Child Left Behind law was putting new pressure on schools to raise student achievement. Matt Hurt, a former special education teacher who would eventually become a central figure in Wise County’s ongoing improvement efforts, saw the new accountability system as an opportunity. Hurt believed students were capable of achieving more. Rather than dwell on the challenges facing Wise County, he wanted to identify the things educators could actually control. That philosophy led to a deceptively simple question: If some teachers were getting extraordinary results with students who weren’t expected to perform well, what were those teachers doing differently? Related These Schools Are Beating the Odds in Teaching Kids to Read This search for best practices eventually grew into the Comprehensive Instructional Program (CIP) , a consortium of Virginia school divisions that now collaborate to improve student achievement. CIP isn’t really a “program” at all. Instead, it provides access to a collection of instructional resources, administers quarterly benchmark assessments, and provides structured opportunities for teachers to learn from one another. Jordan McAlister/Getty Images Most of the materials come from teachers who have already demonstrated success in their own classrooms. For example, literacy teachers can access a year’s worth of standards-aligned “Bell Ringers,” five-minute warm-ups focused on specific phonics or grammar skills. There are also resources for teaching spelling and writing, including exercises that help students build detailed sentences by answering questions like Who? Did what? How? Where? When? and Why?. Teachers can use these materials as needed, rather than following a prescribed curriculum. Taking Standards Seriously Almost every school district claims to be data-driven and standards-aligned. But Wise County takes those ideas further than most. Across the district, teachers administer common benchmark assessments at the end of each quarter in reading, math, science and social studies that are closely aligned with Virginia’s end-of-year state tests, called the Standards of Learning (SOL). CIP staff also check whether those assessments are doing their job. Each year, it compares students’ benchmark results with their eventual state test scores. That allows the consortium to establish targets that can help accurately predict which students are on track to pass the end-of-year state exams. Teachers also have access to pacing guides that recommend how much instructional time to devote to particular standards along the way. Related Top 5 Schools in Each State Beating the Odds in 3rd Grade Reading The process creates a feedback loop where educators teach to the standards, assess student understanding, identify gaps and adjust their instruction or provide extra afterschool support. Hurt describes the benchmark assessments as “biopsies” rather than “autopsies.” Instead of waiting until the end of the year to discover that students have fallen behind, teachers can diagnose problems while there’s still time to do something about them. These are far from revolutionary ideas. But there’s a difference between saying that instruction should be aligned with standards and building an entire ecosystem around making it happen. Of course, critics might call this teaching to the test. When Hurt is pressed on this question, he simply asks, “Which questions on the state test would you not want your own students to be able to answer?” More Than Tests and Data Wise County’s success can’t be fully explained by its benchmark assessments and pacing guides. For example, CIP now serves 83 Virginia school divisions, and not all of them achieve Wise County’s results. The difference may lie in how Wise County combines its instructional systems with a broader culture of support, high expectations and relationships. Marcia Shortt, Wise County’s director of elementary and middle schools and curriculum, describes a deliberate effort to break down the barriers between administrators, school leaders, teachers and parents. “We built a culture that we’re all in this together,” she told me. That collaborative spirit extends to teachers who are struggling. When the quarterly assessments reveal that one teacher’s students are falling behind, district administrators can connect that teacher with a more successful colleague at another school serving a similar population. The district tends to forego external professional development in favor of this local approach. But support doesn’t mean an absence of accountability. Shortt described having difficult conversations with teachers whose students weren’t performing well, including placing some on improvement plans. Wise County expects teachers to deliver results, but it also tries to give them the tools and support to succeed. Related International Literacy Day: 8 Things That Top Schools for Reading Have in Common The district applies a similar philosophy to students. It’s probably no coincidence that Wise’s high school grades are closely aligned with state standards. In the younger grades, students who are struggling can receive targeted tutoring before or after school, with snacks and transportation provided. Students identified as high-risk readers also receive 30 minutes of daily small-group instruction, supported by reading specialists and other staff. And Wise County starts building relationships with families long before children enter kindergarten. The district distributes books and information about its preschool programs to new parents through local hospitals. It also offers storytime events where young children can receive their own books to take home. By the time children enter kindergarten, their families may already have spent two or three years developing relationships with the school system. These efforts appear to be paying off in other ways, too. Last year, only 8% of Wise County students were chronically absent , compared with 13% statewide. None of these practices is particularly revolutionary on its own. But together, they suggest a school system that takes seriously its responsibility to identify problems, provide support and ensure that students succeed. What Can Other Schools Learn from Wise? Wise County’s experience offers a compelling lesson about school improvement. The CIP provides a framework that other districts can use to identify their most successful teachers, have them share their expertise, align instruction to clear expectations and monitor student progress. These are relatively straightforward practices that don’t require flashy new technologies or expensive interventions. But Wise County’s success suggests that the tools alone aren’t enough. District leaders must be willing to confront poor performance, give struggling teachers meaningful support and create a culture where educators see one another as colleagues rather than competitors. And perhaps the most encouraging part of The Wise Rise is that it was far from inevitable. Twenty-five years ago, Wise County’s students were performing below the state average. Today, they are among Virginia’s strongest performers.

title: Most Parents Let Their Young Kids Use Screens. Many Feel Guilty About It
summary: The modern world is replete with screens. That’s true for kids as well as adults. Parents today must decide how much screen time to allow their children at different ages and developmental stages, even as questions about the quality and long-term impacts of digital media persist. Most parents of young children use screens as a […]
content: The modern world is replete with screens. That’s true for kids as well as adults. Parents today must decide how much screen time to allow their children at different ages and developmental stages, even as questions about the quality and long-term impacts of digital media persist. Most parents of young children use screens as a caregiving tool at least some of the time, according to an analysis published this fall by the RAPID Survey Project, based in the Stanford Center on Early Childhood. The data draws upon responses from a national survey of more than 1,000 parents of children ages 6 and under conducted in May 2025 and July 2025. About two-thirds of parents report using screens at least once a week — and sometimes much more frequently — to keep their kids occupied. About two-fifths of parents use screens at least once a week to reward good behavior. And nearly a third of parents use screens to help their child calm down when upset. ( RAPID Survey Project, Stanford Center on Early Childhood ) Phil Fisher, director of the Stanford Center on Early Childhood, said the RAPID findings reveal a tension between the ubiquity of devices in early childhood and the fact that there are risks associated with their use. “Parents are aware of both of those things,” he noted. Open-ended written responses from parents in the survey reveal a second, related tension: Many parents let their children use screens regularly but carry a lot of guilt about that decision. That sentiment was also voiced in parent interviews with The 74, “Screen time is something that I struggle to manage,” a parent in Ohio wrote in the survey. “I feel guilty about letting (my children) use screens, but I also need breaks and screens keep them distracted.” A parent in Minnesota wrote: “I wish my son didn’t use his tablet so much. But it helps him relax after a busy day. It also helps me be able to make meals or do longer chores when he’s occupied with it.” Fisher pointed out that, while there was a time when parents managed to get things done without devices, technology is not the only thing that has changed in recent decades. Related When It Comes to Screen Time, Expert Guidance and Family Realities Diverge “The culture of parenting in this country has changed,” he said. More households today have all available parents in the workforce. And with the cost of living being so high, many parents are working very hard, sometimes in multiple jobs, to make ends meet. “People don’t necessarily want to expend the energy on top of that to be engaged with their child.” “There’s this herd mentality. ‘Everybody else is doing this, and I’m exhausted too. It’s an acceptable thing to do, and so I’ll do it,’” Fisher added. “The changing cultural values and access to technology make it a true dilemma.” Ingrid Gamboa, a working mom of a 7-month-old in Danbury, Connecticut, said she uses screens throughout the week with her daughter to keep her occupied while Gamboa does chores such as cooking and cleaning and to calm her down when she’s upset. During the week, Gamboa works full time while her daughter attends a home-based childcare program, and in the evenings, it’s usually just the two of them. Gamboa’s partner currently works two jobs to support the family financially. She and her daughter don’t see him most days, Gamboa said. After work, Gamboa will turn on the TV for her infant while she gets some chores done, she said. Her daughter watches two programs: “Ms. Rachel,” a YouTube show that is popular among babies and toddlers, and a Spanish-language show called “Plim Plim.” There’s this herd mentality. ‘Everybody else is doing this, and I’m exhausted too. It’s an acceptable thing to do, and so I’ll do it.’ The changing cultural values and access to technology make it a true dilemma. Phil Fisher, director of the Stanford Center on Early Childhood During bathtime and bedtime, sometimes her daughter gets fussy, particularly during transitions. She will resist diaper changes, Gamboa said, or get upset while the bath is being prepared. When that happens, Gamboa will turn the TV on or pull up a video on her phone, knowing that it will settle her daughter right away. “I feel like my problem is that I don’t like her crying,” Gamboa said, “and I found that if I put on a certain show for her, out of nowhere, she stops crying.” Gamboa works for a public school as a home visitor. On her visits with families, parents often voice their concerns with screens, and raise questions about how much screen time to allow their children and what programs are safe or educational. “Now that I live it, it’s difficult,” she said. “It’s one thing telling someone what to do, and another doing it.” She said she now understands the desperation and frustration that parents have expressed to her during home visits. “I sometimes feel guilty because of the knowledge and the background that I have,” Gamboa said. “But at the moment, where I see myself alone, stressed and tired from an eight-hour shift, all I want to do is spend time with (my daughter) and see her smile.” “If my daughter is going to have a hard time with a transition,” she added, “I’d rather give her the phone.” The first three years of life are considered a critical period for learning, noted Sarah Kucker, associate professor of psychology and founder of the Kids in Development Lab at Southern Methodist University in Texas. It’s when children develop their first motor skills, learn to walk and talk, and build social connections. “Every area of development gets a foundation and starts to bloom in those first three years,” Kucker said. “That means every environment children are in should be very supportive of those things.” ( RAPID Survey Project, Stanford Center on Early Childhood ) Today’s technology-driven world can have some benefits for that age, she acknowledged. But it can also detract from really formative physical and social interactions. “Instead of playing with blocks and learning how to stack them, they’re swiping on a tablet,” she said. “That doesn’t teach them quite the same thing.” And instead of talking to and engaging with a caring adult, Kucker said, young kids are increasingly watching a YouTube video or TV show, which can interfere with their language development. For a lot of young kids today, it’s not just direct interactions with media, meaning the times when a child is actively engaging with a screen or device, like watching a cartoon or playing a video game. There are also moments when a child is absorbing media from their environment — maybe a TV is left on in a room where a baby is playing or a parent is working on their laptop during dinner. Kucker recently co-authored a research study which showed that, on top of averaging about two hours per day of direct media use, infants were exposed to another 4.5 hours of indirect media. “The more the kid is sitting in front of a TV and the parent is sitting in front of a phone, it adds up,” she said. Research indicates that when and how digital media is used can dictate its impact. Media used for learning can be effective, especially with some follow-up discussion, Kucker said. A child can watch a video from “Ms. Rachel” and then discuss it with their parent, like, “Oh, you learned about bananas from ‘Ms. Rachel’? Here is a banana to eat, just like she talked about.” “When the technology is replacing some activity or behavior that they need to learn the skill for — like calming themselves down — then they never learn those self-regulation skills,” Kucker said. “That can have cascading effects.” A child who uses screens as a pacifier at age 1 or 2, Kucker said, may have emotion regulation challenges by age 4. ( RAPID Survey Project, Stanford Center on Early Childhood ) Kucker is less concerned about screen time used as a reward or screen time to keep kids occupied, as long as families are smart about how they use it. “What I always say is that if you need to give your kids the tablet for 10 minutes to get dinner ready, and it means you’re going to have a healthy meal, that actually is OK,” she said. “Giving a kid a bag of chips and no media is not better. If you need to give them a tablet for 5 minutes to de-stress or take a shower, that is also better.” For many families, these decisions aren’t clear-cut. In the survey, parents described navigating screen time as an ever-evolving process, even when they felt they were getting it right. “Screen use in our home is something we’re constantly trying to manage thoughtfully,” wrote a parent in Louisiana. “We know screens are a part of modern life, but we try to keep them limited, especially for our child. We notice that too much screen time can affect mood and sleep, so we focus on using screens intentionally for learning or family movie time rather than as a regular distraction. Still, there are times when screens help us get through busy moments, especially when we’re juggling work or household responsibilities.” A parent in California wrote: “I do my absolute best to ensure my kids have healthy habits regarding screen time, but there is no way we could parent without television, as I literally need it to keep my kids occupied.” Related AI ‘Slop’ Is Flooding Children’s Media. Parents Should Be Very Alarmed The issue has reached a point where it’s getting a lot of attention, it’s highly polarizing and people are quick to judge others, said Fisher of Stanford. But he noticed that parents in the survey came down largely in a neutral middle zone, rather than sitting on extreme ends of the spectrum. “There are very few voices saying, ‘It’s evil. I won’t let it in my house. It’s nothing but a negative,’” Fisher said. But neither, he added, are many saying, “I’m all for it. I do it as much as I can.” The reality is, some families turn to screens because it’s an easy and convenient distraction, and others turn to screens out of desperation, because the support system around them is woefully inadequate — from childcare access to everyday affordability. “As a single mom, I can’t take turns with a partner to be the ‘morning person’ or ‘nighttime person,’” a parent in Colorado wrote. “I’m the all-the-time person, and sometimes screen time is the only way I can sleep a little more or clean up and know that my son will be safe and occupied.” Gamboa, who is solo parenting most nights, made a similar point. “When there is a hand to help, I do accept the help, but it’s not that often,” said Gamboa. “If my mom were there, I wouldn’t need to use the videos with my daughter.”

content: The modern world is replete with screens. That’s true for kids as well as adults. Parents today must decide how much screen time to allow their children at different ages and developmental stages, even as questions about the quality and long-term impacts of digital media persist. Most parents of young children use screens as a caregiving tool at least some of the time, according to an analysis published this fall by the RAPID Survey Project, based in the Stanford Center on Early Childhood. The data draws upon responses from a national survey of more than 1,000 parents of children ages 6 and under conducted in May 2025 and July 2025. About two-thirds of parents report using screens at least once a week — and sometimes much more frequently — to keep their kids occupied. About two-fifths of parents use screens at least once a week to reward good behavior. And nearly a third of parents use screens to help their child calm down when upset. ( RAPID Survey Project, Stanford Center on Early Childhood ) Phil Fisher, director of the Stanford Center on Early Childhood, said the RAPID findings reveal a tension between the ubiquity of devices in early childhood and the fact that there are risks associated with their use. “Parents are aware of both of those things,” he noted. Open-ended written responses from parents in the survey reveal a second, related tension: Many parents let their children use screens regularly but carry a lot of guilt about that decision. That sentiment was also voiced in parent interviews with The 74, “Screen time is something that I struggle to manage,” a parent in Ohio wrote in the survey. “I feel guilty about letting (my children) use screens, but I also need breaks and screens keep them distracted.” A parent in Minnesota wrote: “I wish my son didn’t use his tablet so much. But it helps him relax after a busy day. It also helps me be able to make meals or do longer chores when he’s occupied with it.” Fisher pointed out that, while there was a time when parents managed to get things done without devices, technology is not the only thing that has changed in recent decades. Related When It Comes to Screen Time, Expert Guidance and Family Realities Diverge “The culture of parenting in this country has changed,” he said. More households today have all available parents in the workforce. And with the cost of living being so high, many parents are working very hard, sometimes in multiple jobs, to make ends meet. “People don’t necessarily want to expend the energy on top of that to be engaged with their child.” “There’s this herd mentality. ‘Everybody else is doing this, and I’m exhausted too. It’s an acceptable thing to do, and so I’ll do it,’” Fisher added. “The changing cultural values and access to technology make it a true dilemma.” Ingrid Gamboa, a working mom of a 7-month-old in Danbury, Connecticut, said she uses screens throughout the week with her daughter to keep her occupied while Gamboa does chores such as cooking and cleaning and to calm her down when she’s upset. During the week, Gamboa works full time while her daughter attends a home-based childcare program, and in the evenings, it’s usually just the two of them. Gamboa’s partner currently works two jobs to support the family financially. She and her daughter don’t see him most days, Gamboa said. After work, Gamboa will turn on the TV for her infant while she gets some chores done, she said. Her daughter watches two programs: “Ms. Rachel,” a YouTube show that is popular among babies and toddlers, and a Spanish-language show called “Plim Plim.” There’s this herd mentality. ‘Everybody else is doing this, and I’m exhausted too. It’s an acceptable thing to do, and so I’ll do it.’ The changing cultural values and access to technology make it a true dilemma. Phil Fisher, director of the Stanford Center on Early Childhood During bathtime and bedtime, sometimes her daughter gets fussy, particularly during transitions. She will resist diaper changes, Gamboa said, or get upset while the bath is being prepared. When that happens, Gamboa will turn the TV on or pull up a video on her phone, knowing that it will settle her daughter right away. “I feel like my problem is that I don’t like her crying,” Gamboa said, “and I found that if I put on a certain show for her, out of nowhere, she stops crying.” Gamboa works for a public school as a home visitor. On her visits with families, parents often voice their concerns with screens, and raise questions about how much screen time to allow their children and what programs are safe or educational. “Now that I live it, it’s difficult,” she said. “It’s one thing telling someone what to do, and another doing it.” She said she now understands the desperation and frustration that parents have expressed to her during home visits. “I sometimes feel guilty because of the knowledge and the background that I have,” Gamboa said. “But at the moment, where I see myself alone, stressed and tired from an eight-hour shift, all I want to do is spend time with (my daughter) and see her smile.” “If my daughter is going to have a hard time with a transition,” she added, “I’d rather give her the phone.” The first three years of life are considered a critical period for learning, noted Sarah Kucker, associate professor of psychology and founder of the Kids in Development Lab at Southern Methodist University in Texas. It’s when children develop their first motor skills, learn to walk and talk, and build social connections. “Every area of development gets a foundation and starts to bloom in those first three years,” Kucker said. “That means every environment children are in should be very supportive of those things.” ( RAPID Survey Project, Stanford Center on Early Childhood ) Today’s technology-driven world can have some benefits for that age, she acknowledged. But it can also detract from really formative physical and social interactions. “Instead of playing with blocks and learning how to stack them, they’re swiping on a tablet,” she said. “That doesn’t teach them quite the same thing.” And instead of talking to and engaging with a caring adult, Kucker said, young kids are increasingly watching a YouTube video or TV show, which can interfere with their language development. For a lot of young kids today, it’s not just direct interactions with media, meaning the times when a child is actively engaging with a screen or device, like watching a cartoon or playing a video game. There are also moments when a child is absorbing media from their environment — maybe a TV is left on in a room where a baby is playing or a parent is working on their laptop during dinner. Kucker recently co-authored a research study which showed that, on top of averaging about two hours per day of direct media use, infants were exposed to another 4.5 hours of indirect media. “The more the kid is sitting in front of a TV and the parent is sitting in front of a phone, it adds up,” she said. Research indicates that when and how digital media is used can dictate its impact. Media used for learning can be effective, especially with some follow-up discussion, Kucker said. A child can watch a video from “Ms. Rachel” and then discuss it with their parent, like, “Oh, you learned about bananas from ‘Ms. Rachel’? Here is a banana to eat, just like she talked about.” “When the technology is replacing some activity or behavior that they need to learn the skill for — like calming themselves down — then they never learn those self-regulation skills,” Kucker said. “That can have cascading effects.” A child who uses screens as a pacifier at age 1 or 2, Kucker said, may have emotion regulation challenges by age 4. ( RAPID Survey Project, Stanford Center on Early Childhood ) Kucker is less concerned about screen time used as a reward or screen time to keep kids occupied, as long as families are smart about how they use it. “What I always say is that if you need to give your kids the tablet for 10 minutes to get dinner ready, and it means you’re going to have a healthy meal, that actually is OK,” she said. “Giving a kid a bag of chips and no media is not better. If you need to give them a tablet for 5 minutes to de-stress or take a shower, that is also better.” For many families, these decisions aren’t clear-cut. In the survey, parents described navigating screen time as an ever-evolving process, even when they felt they were getting it right. “Screen use in our home is something we’re constantly trying to manage thoughtfully,” wrote a parent in Louisiana. “We know screens are a part of modern life, but we try to keep them limited, especially for our child. We notice that too much screen time can affect mood and sleep, so we focus on using screens intentionally for learning or family movie time rather than as a regular distraction. Still, there are times when screens help us get through busy moments, especially when we’re juggling work or household responsibilities.” A parent in California wrote: “I do my absolute best to ensure my kids have healthy habits regarding screen time, but there is no way we could parent without television, as I literally need it to keep my kids occupied.” Related AI ‘Slop’ Is Flooding Children’s Media.
